item.title: Taveuni businessman puts jobs and families at the heart of business growth
item.description: Creating employment opportunities, supporting local families and improving access to goods and services in Taveuni remain key priorities for Sun City Supermarket Managing Director Rohil Chaudhari, as he continues to grow his business on the island. Chaudhari operates three Sun City Supermarket stores in Wairiki, Naqara and Matei, providing employment for 38 full-time staff, with women making up ap
item.content:encoded:
Creating employment opportunities, supporting local families and improving access to goods and services in Taveuni remain key priorities for Sun City Supermarket Managing Director Rohil Chaudhari, as he continues to grow his business on the island.

Chaudhari operates three Sun City Supermarket stores in Wairiki, Naqara and Matei, providing employment for 38 full-time staff, with women making up approximately 70 percent of the workforce.

He says creating jobs for local people is an important part of his business, as it also helps support their families and the wider community.

Chaudhari says he believes women are capable of taking on important roles in the business, and is proud of the strong team of women working across his stores.

He says building the business has not been easy, but adapting to change and receiving strong support from the community have helped his operations grow over the years.

To improve access to goods and services, Chaudhari has also invested in the company's own transport system, including two 12-wheeler trucks and a freezer truck, to move goods from Suva to Taveuni.

He says this helps save time and allows the business to offer customers products and services similar to those available on the mainland.

The business has also introduced a fully electric vehicle for its operations around Taveuni.

Chaudhari says the electric vehicle is the company's first step towards reducing its carbon footprint, improving efficiency and lowering operating costs.

He says his focus is to continue introducing new ideas, technology and services that benefit his customers while creating more opportunities for the people of Taveuni.

item.title: National tender planned for medical equipment after CWM patient monitor shortage issue
item.description: The Ministry of Health is preparing a national tender for the replacement of patient monitoring machines and other essential medical equipment following concerns over ageing monitors and shortages at CWM Hospital’s Emergency Department. When questioned by fijivillage News, Assistant Minister for Health, Penioni Ravunawa says that there was no separate budget for patient monitoring machines at CWM
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of Health is preparing a national tender for the replacement of patient monitoring machines and other essential medical equipment following concerns over ageing monitors and shortages at CWM Hospital’s Emergency Department.

When questioned by fijivillage News, Assistant Minister for Health, Penioni Ravunawa says that there was no separate budget for patient monitoring machines at CWM Hospital’s Emergency Department, with funding managed through the Ministry of Health’s broader biomedical equipment allocation.

He says the Ministry acknowledges that the ageing patient monitors at CWM Hospital should have been replaced earlier, and the delay reflects a long-standing backlog of ageing medical equipment, limited capital funding, competing clinical priorities and lengthy procurement processes.

He says Fiji imports virtually all biomedical equipment and spare parts, which adds to costs and affects delivery timelines.

The Ministry’s response comes after fijivillage raised questions about why the CWM Emergency Department had only three patient monitors and what is being done to address the shortage and replace the ageing equipment.

The department has since received 10 new patient monitors donated by the International Women’s Association and GE Healthcare.

IWA President Judy Compain had earlier revealed that she witnessed two patients being resuscitated at the hospital, with staff having to move monitors between them.

Compain says she later contacted a doctor to find out how many monitors were available in the Emergency Department and was told there were only three.

She says after discussions with the hospital about its equipment needs, the decision was made to provide 10 new monitors.

CWM Hospital Chief Medical Officer Dr Deepak Sharma had also confirmed that the previous monitors were installed around 2013 to 2014 and had gone well beyond their intended period of use.

He says there had been several roadblocks and challenges in securing new monitors, but the department has received new monitors for patients in the resuscitation area, as well as mobile monitors.

Dr Sharma says the old equipment had supported the department through the COVID-19 pandemic, but it was time for the monitors to be replaced.

He says the donated equipment includes monitors for patients in the resuscitation area and mobile monitors that will allow staff to continue monitoring patients throughout the Emergency Department, particularly when patient movement is restricted by overcrowding and access block.

Meanwhile, Ravunawa says the Ministry is preparing a national tender to purchase and replace patient monitoring machines and other essential medical equipment across the public health system.

He says the programme will cover tertiary and divisional hospitals, subdivisional hospitals, health centres, nursing stations and outreach services.

The replacement programme will be implemented in phases over five years, with the Ministry taking into account available funding, installation capacity, staff training and long-term maintenance support.

Ravunawa says the Ministry is also seeking quotations to provide immediate relief at facilities where equipment shortages or failures pose the greatest clinical risk, including CWM Hospital.

He says the Ministry is strengthening its national equipment inventory and condition assessments, prioritising replacements according to clinical risk and standardising equipment specifications to prevent similar shortages in the future.

Future procurement will also include warranties, servicing, spare parts, consumables and staff training to ensure new machines remain functional throughout their expected service life.

In response to questions from fijivillage, Minister for Health Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu had earlier said the Ministry has a budgeted equipment purchase and replacement programme, which is currently being funded and implemented by FPBS.

Dr Lalabalavu cited the replacement of floor-mounted and ceiling-mounted X-ray machines in tertiary and subdivisional hospitals as one example of the programme.

He says almost $5 million in Government funding has been committed to transitioning from analogue to digital X-ray equipment, in collaboration with FPBS, a local supplier, the National Adviser on Radiology and medical imaging technologists.

The Minister says the initiative reflects the Government’s commitment to listening to technical staff about their equipment needs and providing the necessary funding.

Ravunawa says the Ministry appreciates the assistance provided by organisations, corporate partners and development partners, but stresses that such support does not replace the Government’s responsibility to invest in and sustain the public health system.

He says the Ministry recognises the public expects critical medical equipment to be available when needed and accepts its responsibility to address existing gaps while implementing a sustainable national replacement programme within its available budget.

The Ministry is also encouraging Fijians to make healthier choices, follow professional medical advice and use primary healthcare and outpatient services appropriately to help reduce avoidable pressure on emergency departments.

However, it acknowledges that preventive healthcare does not replace the need for safe and properly equipped medical facilities.

item.title: Dakuitoga calls for clear commitment on next general elections date
item.description: The Government is being urged to provide a clear commitment on when Fijis next general elections will be held and ensure the proposed constitutional changes do not delay the election or extend Parliaments term. Content creator and influencer Eliki Dakuitoga shared this before the Joint Parliamentary Select Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 at Vunimono Hall in Nausori, calling for
item.content:encoded:
The Government is being urged to provide a clear commitment on when Fijis next general elections will be held and ensure the proposed constitutional changes do not delay the election or extend Parliaments term.

Content creator and influencer Eliki Dakuitoga shared this before the Joint Parliamentary Select Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 at Vunimono Hall in Nausori, calling for stronger legal safeguards to protect the next elections.

Dakuitoga says the existing lawful deadline for the election must be clearly protected in legislation, even if the new Constitution comes into effect earlier than expected.

He is seeking clarification on Section 219, saying the proposed provision should not restart Parliaments four-year term, revive an expired or dissolved Parliament, or allow it to continue without a general election.

Dakuitoga also wants the committee to explain how the proposed Section 211, which allows the President to bring the new Constitution into effect earlier through a proclamation published in the Gazette, would affect the election timetable.

He says the committee must clearly identify which electoral system, nomination requirements, polling rules and deadlines will apply to the next general elections, particularly if constitutional changes take effect while election preparations are already underway.

He is also raising concerns about the proposed emergency powers under Section 201, saying these must not be used to extend Parliaments term or delay an election for political reasons.

Using a severe cyclone as an example, Dakuitoga says there must be clear legal procedures for dealing with genuine disruptions to polling, including who can authorise a delay, the reasons required, independent scrutiny and access to the courts.

He is asking the Government to confirm whether the election will be held in 2026 or January 2027, and if not, to confirm that it will take place no later than 6th February 2027, which he identifies as the last possible date published by election authorities.

Dakuitoga says the preparation of a new Constitution or electoral system should not, by itself, justify extending the current parliamentary term.

He is also calling for the final wording of the relevant constitutional provisions to be published, together with a clear explanation of how the changes would affect the election under either outcome of a possible referendum.

Dakuitoga says the public needs certainty about the election timetable, the applicable laws and the safeguards that will prevent any misuse of constitutional or emergency powers.

item.title: Residents in the west seek help as termite damage worsens in homes
item.description: Residents across the Western Division are raising concerns over extensive termite damage to their homes, with some houses reportedly deteriorating to the point where they have been advised to be burnt down. Speaking to fijivillage News, Navneet Ram says the situation has worsened, with termites causing significant damage to homes and their structures.
item.content:encoded:
Residents across the Western Division are raising concerns over extensive termite damage to their homes, with some houses reportedly deteriorating to the point where they have been advised to be burnt down.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Navneet Ram says the situation has worsened, with termites causing significant damage to homes and their structures.

He says termite infestations can cause extensive structural damage over time, potentially leaving homeowners facing costly repairs or the need to replace damaged structures.

Ram says the problem, previously concentrated in Lautoka, has spread to other parts of the West, including Ba.

Ram says some residents light fires every evening in an effort to reduce termite activity, however, the problem remains persistent.

He is calling on relevant government authorities to assist families whose homes have suffered extensive termite damage.

Questions have been sent to Biosecurity Authority Fiji.
